newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S., Russian soldiers patrol tense village.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russian soldiers patrol tense village.

text.p: U.S. and Russian troops helped defuse a tense confrontation between groups of Bosnian Moslems and Serbs near a village in northeast Bosnia on Wednesday, the NATO-led peace force reported.

American and Russian peacekeeping troops deployed between a crowd of about 100 Moslems and some 200 Serbs near the contested village of Gajevi to prevent possible violence, a U.S. officer told Reuters.
Tensions have been running high along the former front line where Moslems have tried to cross to return to their pre-war homes.
The peacekeeping troops tried to cool tempers by talking to the two groups, who were separated by some 100 metres (yards), said the officer from the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
"The U.S. soldiers were talking to the Moslems trying to calm them down and the Russians were trying to calm the Serbs down," said the officer, who asked not to be named.
Reporters at the scene saw Serb protesters clad in nationalist "Cetnik" garb, some of them wielding knives, taunting Moslems with nationalist songs.

At one point the commanding U.S. officer in the northeast region, U.S. Major General Montgomery Meigs, ordered platoons of American tanks, military police and Bradley fighting vehicles to prepare to move into the area.
As the reinforcements were en route from a base south of Tuzla, the crowds began to disperse and Meigs called off the deployment, the officer said.
Bosnian Moslems have demanded to move back to their homes in Gajevi, which lies in Bosnia's Serb republic, but local Serb residents have threatened to stop them.
Moslems say they want to fulfil their right under the Dayton peace accords to return to their homes.
Serb authorities allege the move is an armed instrusion into conquered territory purged of Moslems and Croats.
U.N. relief officials said 36 Moslem families had planned to enter Gajevi this week after submitting to a procedure supervised by international agencies.
An advance team had hoped to enter Gajevi on Wednesday to begin construction work on temporary housing but the confrontation scuppered that plan.
A firefight erupted in November in the village when Moslems tried to enter. A Serb man died and two Moslems were wounded in the violence.
U.S. and Russian soldiers saw no sign that either side was armed in Wednesday's confrontation, the officer said. "There were absolutely no weapons in evidence."
A bridge near Gajevi was damaged in an explosion over the weekend and another explosion was reported on Tuesday night on a track leading to the village, according to SFOR.
Another bridge was possibly damaged in Tuesday's blast but Russian soldiers were unable to investigate the explosion because local residents said the area was mined.
U.S. and Russian soldiers, who have recently launched joint weekly patrols, are now conducting daily joint patrols in the Gajevi region to prevent possible violence.
A U.S.-Russian patrol found a newly-laid explosive device in the area this week. It appeared to be a booby-trap but there were no other details immediately available, SFOR officers said.
